[Thinking]
**Planning a ghost story**

I need to create a concise yet comprehensive story, aiming for about 1200 to 2000 words. I’m focusing on an ancient China ghost story, which means I should weave in cultural elements and a captivating atmosphere. It's great to balance detail without getting too verbose, so I’ll ensure to moderate my approach. Let’s move ahead with crafting this intriguing tale, inviting both mystery and cultural depth. I’m excited to see how it unfolds!
[/Thinking]

The winter wind slid down from the northern mountains and scraped its cold fingers over the walls of Yanshui Prefecture. By dusk, the streets had emptied; the wine sellers shuttered their doors, and the watchmen hurried to hang their lanterns early. For three nights now, strange cries had risen from the old examination compound on the eastern outskirts of the city—cries that sounded like weeping, like the shredding of silk, like ink grinding on stone.

The magistrate, Lord Wei, was not a man easily frightened. He had been a district official in border regions where bandits set fields on fire and wolves carried off children. But ghosts were different. You could negotiate with bandits, track wolves. Ghosts belonged to Heaven’s ledger, not his.

Yet the complaints would not stop. The prefecture test for scholars was only a month away, and the young hopefuls were already gathering. Each night, students lodged near the compound claimed they heard voices reciting poetry in the dark, interrupted by a choking gurgle, then pounding at the locked doors. Others swore they saw a pale figure sitting at the empty desks inside, gazing at a scroll that dripped black.

On the fourth morning, when a group of terrified scholars stormed his yamen and knelt in the courtyard, Lord Wei summoned his secretary.

“Fetch that village Daoist,” he said. “The one who counts turtle shells and reads the stars.”

“Humble Prefect,” the secretary began delicately, “Daoist Qiu is away in the mountains observing an auspicious constellation. However…” He cleared his throat. “There is a scholar in the outer lodgings. A failed candidate from the last sitting. He has read widely in the *Yi Jing*, the *Zuo Tradition*, even the strange ghost tales of old. The students trust him. His name is Wen Shun.”

“A failed candidate,” Lord Wei muttered. “The city is full of failed candidates.” But the prefectural exam was everything here; if fear kept students away, his own record would suffer. “Fine. Summon this Wen Shun. Let us see what use bookworms are against spirits.”

***

Wen Shun bowed in the magistrate’s hall, his robe patched but clean, his hair pinned with an old wooden stick. At twenty-eight, he had already failed the county and prefecture examinations three times. His family’s fields back in Gansu had been sold to pay his travel and study, and his father’s letters had grown shorter every year.

Lord Wei studied him. “You hear of ghosts in the examination compound, and instead of running home, you stay here. Why?”

Wen Shun pressed his forehead to the tiles. “This lowly one has nothing to return to, My Lord. If the spirits are learned, perhaps I may ask them how to pass the exams.”

One of the clerks snorted, earning a sharp glance. Lord Wei’s mouth twitched.

“You joke before the ink is dry on the accusations. Are you not afraid?”

“Afraid, of course.” Wen Shun raised his head. “But the sages teach that ghosts and spirits are manifestations of *qi*. If one understands their grievances, one can persuade them. Moreover”—he paused—“if the compound remains haunted, the exam may be postponed. Then all will suffer. I have studied the rites, old exorcistic formulae, and the chronicles of strange events. Allow me to go and see.”

“You talk like a commentator on the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,” Lord Wei said. “Very well. Tonight you will keep watch in the examination yard. I will lend you two night-watch soldiers, but remember, swords cannot cut what does not bleed. If you can resolve this matter, I will personally sponsor you for recommendation beyond this prefecture.”

Wen Shun’s heart kicked in his chest like a trapped bird. He kowtowed three times till his forehead stung. “This unworthy one will obey.”

***

The examination compound crouched outside the east gate, a long rectangle of high walls and plain tiled roofs. Inside were rows upon rows of narrow cells—brick cubicles barely big enough for a man to sit and write, each with a wooden plank for a desk and a ledge for sleeping. Under the moonlight, it looked like a cemetery with its graves laid open.

The gatekeeper, an old cripple with one blind eye, refused to step near after dusk.

“Since the snow last year,” he rasped, clutching his hemp coat, “this place has changed. At night I hear someone grinding ink, grinding and grinding, but by morning there is not a mark on any desk. Then sobbing… then a long sigh, like air leaving a bellows. When I try to sleep, I feel fingers combing my hair.”

The two soldiers Lord Wei had assigned stood on either side of Wen Shun as the gate clanged shut behind them. Their spears dipped slightly.

“Scholar Wen,” one muttered, “rule of the camp: if anything calls your name, don’t answer.”

“And if something asks what time it is,” said the other, “never tell.”

“How do I address you both?” Wen Shun asked.

“Zhang,” said the first.

“Also Zhang,” said the second.

“In that case,” Wen Shun said dryly, “I will shout ‘Zhang’ and trust that at least one of you comes.”

The moon sailed west; the winter stars pierced the sky like nails. The three of them sat beneath the eaves of the main hall, a brazier of charcoal between them. Above the door, a wooden plaque read: “Hall of Verifying Talents.”

“You two stay here,” Wen Shun said as the night deepened. “If something happens, you will hear me.”

“You go alone?” one of the Zhangs asked, knuckles whitening on his spear.

“If the spirit is bound by grievance, too many people may frighten it,” Wen Shun replied. “Besides, you are soldiers of the prefecture. If you flee, who will be left to ring the alarm?”

He wrapped his threadbare cloak tighter and walked into the rows of exam cells. His breath smoked in the air. The compound smelled of old ink, rat droppings, and the faint metallic tang of weathered iron locks.

At first, there was nothing but the creak of wood cooling, the whisper of the wind over the walls. Then, as the moon tipped over the edge of the sky, he heard it.

Scrape. Scrape. Scrape.

It came from the center of the yard, a careful, measured sound, as of someone grinding an ink stick in a stone mortar. Wen Shun’s scalp prickled. He forced himself closer, passing cell after cell.

From one cubicle, cold air exhaled against his cheek. Inside, a lone inkstone sat on the desk. Water glistened in its hollow, black and viscous. The stick, worn thin as a finger, moved back and forth though no hand held it.

Scrape. Scrape.

Wen Shun swallowed. “Honored one,” he said, bowing toward the little desk, “this humble scholar Wen Shun intrudes. Might I know the family name and given name of the gentleman studying so diligently by night?”

The ink stick halted. Silence pooled in the air, thick as congealed blood. Then a voice sounded behind him.

“Names?” it said in a hoarse whisper. “What use have the dead for names?”

Wen Shun turned slowly.

The figure stood in the narrow corridor, barely an arm’s width away. It wore the cotton robe of a poor student, soaked down the front as if it had walked through a river. The cloth was stiff and dark in the moonlight, hanging in stiff ripples. The face… the face was pale as unpainted porcelain, the lips tinged blue. But what froze Wen Shun was the neck. Around it a livid red mark wrapped like a rope, and just above that, the skin was torn and gouged, as if nails had dug in and pulled.

The ghost’s eyes were bloodshot and bulged, still bearing the struggle of its last moments.

Wen Shun’s knees wanted to fold, but he pressed his nails into his palms until he felt the skin break. “You must have been a hard reader in life,” he forced himself to say. “To still sit among the cells you left.”

“I left?” The ghost laughed, high and thin. “I never left. They carried my body out, but I remained.”

He drifted closer. Wen Shun smelled stagnant river water and the mold of old books.

“They say those who die unburied become wild ghosts,” Wen Shun said. “Yet you stand here in scholar’s dress. Were you not given the rites?”

The ghost’s expression twisted. “A rough coffin. A ditch at the back of the compound. No incense. No mourning. Only the clatter of the clerk’s abacus, counting the silver they saved.”

Wen Shun bowed deeper. “Then injustice has bound you. Tell me your grievance. If it lies within the power of men to cleanse it, I will petition the magistrate.”

The ghost watched him. Something like a smile pulled at his cracked lips.

“You speak like you write eight-legged essays,” he said. “Always with the correct order of phrases. Listen then, to my eight legs of suffering.

“First leg: poverty. My name in life was Liang Song. My father was a boatman on the Luo River. I ate coarse millet until I was twelve, when a retired scholar noticed me memorizing poems while helping unload his trunks. He gave me old books. I studied by lamplight, burning reeds, because we had no oil.

“Second leg: duty. My father sold our small plot of land for me to come here the first time. ‘If one of us enters officialdom,’ he said, ‘your younger sisters will no longer need to bind their feet to marry well.’

“Third leg: perseverance. I failed the county exams once, twice. Each time I returned, I studied, I came again. Each time I wrote till my fingers cramped and my ink froze on the brush.

“Fourth leg: betrayal.”

The ghost’s voice thickened. He drifted past Wen Shun and into the cell, his form half-passing through the bricks. The ink stick shuddered and stilled.

“It was last winter,” Liang Song said. “Snow thick as rice husks. We sat in these cells for three days, writing till our breath smoked and stuck to the page. But I… I had no money left for proper food. I ate cold pancakes, moldy beans. On the second night, my head ached, my vision blurred. I miswrote a classic quote. I knew then that my chance was lost.

“In despair, I left my cell. The river beyond the east wall ran black and silent. I climbed onto the parapet. Below, the ice grinned with its broken teeth. I thought: if I jump, I need think no more of commentary or quotas, of tutors and examiners and my father’s bowed back.”

He touched his torn neck absently.

“But as I stood there, I heard voices from the main hall. Our prefect at that time, Lord Zhao, was speaking with the chief examiner. I crept closer.

“‘This Liang Song from Luo River,’ the examiner said. ‘His essay shows promise. With guidance, he could climb high.’

“‘Promise?’ Lord Zhao snorted. ‘His father is a boatman. There is no one to recommend him, no patron to credit. If I advance such a one, what profit is there? Better the son of Magistrate Lu in the next district. His essay is mediocre, but his family…’

“They laughed. Laughed. I pressed my ear to the window lattice and heard the shuffle of silver ingots passed across the table.

“Then I knew. My failure was not Heaven’s test, not an honest trial of talent. It was bought and traded like a sack of grain.”

Wen Shun felt cold creep into his marrow.

“So I did not jump of my own will,” Liang Song whispered. “I walked back to my cell. I tied the cord of my bedding around the beam. When my feet kicked at the bricks, the last thing I saw was my essay lying open on the desk, the ink not yet dry.

“Fifth leg: neglect. They found me at dawn. The keeper cursed, for it was ill luck. He dragged me out by my ankles. The assistant examiner said, ‘Quickly bury him; the others will be disturbed.’ No priest. No petitions to my family. They stuffed me into a rough box and tipped me into a frozen ditch at the back. My soul, chained by bitter *qi*, could not depart.

“Sixth leg: silence. For a year, I wandered this compound. The new candidates buried their noses in their books. When the lanterns were out, I whispered hints at their ears, lines of history, phrases of the classics. Some passed with flying colors. They burned incense for their ancestors, not knowing who had guided their hand.”

Liang Song’s broken mouth curled. “Still I could not leave. The ditch soaked me with meltwater each spring. Worms chewed my bones. My name faded from the registry.”

“Seventh leg: return. This year, they rebuilt the eastern wall. When the workers dug, they unearthed my coffin. I heard them shout. ‘A suicide from the exams, eh? Bad omen!’ They did not rebury me with care. They smashed the box, scattered what they did not want to touch. So my bones lie in the weeds, my spirit in the halls. The compound has become my tomb and my prison.

“Eighth leg: envy.” His eyes flared dull red. “I watch them come, year after year. Sons of merchants and magistrates, complaining that the cells are cramped, that the food is poor, that three days is long to write. They have warm cloaks and fat ink sticks, pockets full of coins for bribes. They pass, and their names are hung in gold characters. Who remembers Liang Song of Luo River?

“So I began to knock at the doors. To whisper at their windows: ‘Why study? Why try? The list is already written in silver.’ Some went mad, tearing up their essays. Others fled in the night. Their fear is a small repayment.”

Wen Shun listened, his own past failures weighing like lead. He thought of late nights under sputtering lamps, of his father’s quiet, the disappointed silence that filled each corner of their clay-walled home.

“Liang gongzi,” he said quietly, “if injustice chained you, then justice may yet unbind.”

The ghost gave a rasping laugh. “Justice? From men like Lord Zhao?”

“Lord Zhao is dead,” Wen Shun said. “Our current magistrate is Lord Wei. He is strict, but not known for greed. If he hears this, he may—”

“May what?” Liang Song snapped. “Give me a posthumous eighth place? Build a wooden tablet and bow to it twice a year? What use is that in the Yellow Springs?”

“For the living,” Wen Shun said, lifting his gaze to meet the ghost’s bulging eyes, “it may change the path. If the corruption is punished, future Liangs will not have to hang themselves in narrow cells. And for you… if your story is acknowledged by law, your resentment may lessen. You might find a boat across the dark river.”

The wind shifted. For a heartbeat, the ghost’s form wavered.

“You speak so confidently,” Liang murmured. “And what of you, Wen Shun? Failed three times, is it not so? If you expose this, you may bring the whole examination system here under scrutiny. They may cancel this year’s sitting. You may lose your last chance of youth.”

Wen Shun’s heart pounded. Images flashed: his father’s stooped back, his sisters’ calloused hands, the neighbors’ mutters. The hope that had kept him alive all these years was a small, tattered thing, but it burned stubbornly.

He inhaled the iron-cold air.

“If the ladder is rotten,” he said slowly, “what honor is there in climbing it? Better to mend it, even if I never reach the top. Our teacher in the village school once said: ‘To learn and not practice what is right is like not learning at all.’ Let me at least do this one sentence correctly.”

Liang Song stared at him for a long time. The ink in the stone had dried; cracks crazed its surface.

“Very well,” the ghost said at last, his voice thin as a breeze through reeds. “Go to your magistrate. Speak my name. Have them fetch what bones they can find, bury them with rites as for a wronged soul. Have them mark in the records that Liang Song of Luo River was unjustly treated by Examiners Zhao and his ilk. Invite my father’s shade to know.

“If all this is done, I will believe that the world of sun and dust can still hear the cries of the buried. Until then, I will walk here.”

He leaned forward, the cold of his presence stabbing through Wen Shun’s skull. “But heed this: if they mock you, if they turn this into another jest over wine, I will come to your bedside. Together we will wander these rows until the tiles crumble.”

Wen Shun’s mouth had gone dry. He bowed low enough that his forehead brushed the frozen brick.

“I will return by tomorrow night,” he said.

When he straightened, the corridor was empty. The inkstone was dry and cracked. Somewhere in the distance, a watchman beat the third night-watch drum.

***

Lord Wei listened, fingers steepled, as Wen Shun spoke in the cold morning light. The magistrate’s hall was warmer than the exam compound, but Wen Shun’s hands still shook; he clutched his sleeve to hide it.

“Liang Song,” Lord Wei repeated. “A suicide in the previous prefect’s term.”

He called for the old records. Clerks lugged out bamboo-bound volumes smelling of mold. After an hour, they found it: a brief note in a margin, written in a bored hand.

“‘One student, name Liang, hanged himself in cell 438 during last winter’s examination. Body interred near east wall. Omens consulted: no ill portents detected.’”

Lord Wei’s jaw tightened. He stood abruptly.

“Summon the gatekeeper. And the workmen who rebuilt the wall.”

By noon, several men knelt, trembling, in the courtyard. Under Lord Wei’s cold questions, the story of Liang Song’s shabby burial tumbled out. The lead worker admitted to breaking open the coffin and discarding scattered bones.

“That is enough,” Lord Wei said, disgust sharpening his voice. “We will search the grounds behind the east wall. Every fragment we find will be gathered. The rites must be performed.”

He turned to Wen Shun. “And the corruption. You implicate my predecessor, Lord Zhao, and his chief examiner. The ghost’s words cannot serve directly as evidence in a court of law. But missing silver leaves trails. Clerks remember. Servants talk. I will investigate this matter. If your account of Liang Song’s grievances proves true, we will memorialize it to the provincial office.”

Wen Shun bowed to the floor. “Even if Your Excellency only gives him proper burial, Liang Song’s soul will know.”

Lord Wei looked down at him. “You risked much, spending the night there. Why come back to tell me, when silence would have been safer?”

Wen Shun looked up, his eyes clear despite the exhaustion.

“My Lord, we are taught that officialdom is the road by which the worthy assist the people,” he said. “Yet the road is lined with bleached bones. If we avert our eyes from even one, what right have we to call ourselves scholars?”

Lord Wei’s gaze lingered. Then he nodded once.

“The rites will be performed tonight,” he said. “You will join them. A wronged scholar should be appeased by another scholar.”

***

As the sun slid toward the western hills, a procession wound out of Yanshui’s east gate: Lord Wei in court robes, clerks with scrolls and tall hats, Daoist acolytes with bells and wooden fish-drums, and Wen Shun carrying a brazier of incense.

Behind the examination compound, the ground was half-frozen and pitted with old construction. Laborers had marked a circle where they’d found shards of coffin-board and splinters of bone. Now, in the cold twilight, those fragments lay arranged on a blue cloth.

The Daoist priest chanted from the *Jade Register of the Dead*, calling on officials of the underworld to witness. Paper money fluttered up in gray flakes as assistants burned it, sending ghostly coin to the other side.

Lord Wei stepped forward and knelt, touching his forehead to the earth three times before the bones.

“Liang Song of Luo River,” he said, his voice carrying into the chill air, “hear this magistrate’s words. The world of yang acknowledges that you suffered grievance here. This district bears you apology. We now bury your remains within the protective wall, with incense and rites as for a wronged soul. May your spirit pass to where there is no cold nor hunger, and may you no longer wander among ink and dust.”

He rose. At his gesture, workers lowered a proper coffin into a freshly dug grave. Wen Shun stepped up, holding a tablet inscribed with four characters: “Tomb of the Wronged Scholar.”

He planted it in the earth as the soil thudded down.

When the last clod fell and the incense smoke twisted in the dimming air, a faint wind moved through the leafless willows. Wen Shun felt it brush his cheek: not the knife-like chill of the night before, but a cool, ordinary breeze.

In the slightest hush between the Daoist’s chants, he thought he heard a voice, very far away, reciting the opening line of the *Book of Songs*:

“Guan-guan cry the ospreys, on the islet in the river…”

Then it faded.

***

That night, Wen Shun went again to the examination compound, this time voluntarily. The two Zhang soldiers refused to leave the gate, muttering that one success should not tempt fate. Wen Shun walked alone through the rows of cells under a sky like hammered iron.

No ink stick scraped. No unseen fingers brushed his hair. The cells were only empty rooms, cold and dull, waiting to swallow the dreams of the living.

He stood before Liang Song’s old cubicle—cell 438—and bowed deeply.

“If you have truly gone on,” he said softly, “then listen to my foolish request from afar. Lend me a phrase or two, perhaps, when I sit here next month.”

Nothing answered. The silence felt, for the first time, like peace.

***

The investigation into Lord Zhao’s tenure uncovered a nest of bribery and favoritism. Ledgers showed inexplicable silver income; testimonies from embittered servants revealed years of purchased places on the lists. The provincial authorities, once alerted, made a show of righteousness: posthumous censures were issued, confiscated wealth used to repair schools and buy grain.

In the corner of one long memorial, however, a single line mentioned “Liang Song of Luo River, whose unjust death drew down misfortune and whose grievance has now been redressed

“In despair, I left my cell. The river beyond the east wall ran black and silent. I climbed onto the parapet. Below, the ice grinned with its broken teeth. I thought: if I jump, I need think no more of commentary or quotas, of tutors and examiners and my father’s bowed back.”

He touched his torn neck absently.

“But as I stood there, I heard voices from the main hall. Our prefect at that time, Lord Zhao, was speaking with the chief examiner. I crept closer.

“‘This Liang Song from Luo River,’ the examiner said. ‘His essay shows promise. With guidance, he could climb high.’

“‘Promise?’ Lord Zhao snorted. ‘His father is a boatman. There is no one to recommend him, no patron to credit. If I advance such a one, what profit is there? Better the son of Magistrate Lu in the next district. His essay is mediocre, but his family…’

“They laughed. Laughed. I pressed my ear to the window lattice and heard the shuffle of silver ingots passed across the table.

“Then I knew. My failure was not Heaven’s test, not an honest trial of talent. It was bought and traded like a sack of grain.”

Wen Shun felt cold creep into his marrow.

“So I did not jump of my own will,” Liang Song whispered. “I walked back to my cell. I tied the cord of my bedding around the beam. When my feet kicked at the bricks, the last thing I saw was my essay lying open on the desk, the ink not yet dry.

“Fifth leg: neglect. They found me at dawn. The keeper cursed, for it was ill luck. He dragged me out by my ankles. The assistant examiner said, ‘Quickly bury him; the others will be disturbed.’ No priest. No petitions to my family. They stuffed me into a rough box and tipped me into a frozen ditch at the back. My soul, chained by bitter *qi*, could not depart.

“Sixth leg: silence. For a year, I wandered this compound. The new candidates buried their noses in their books. When the lanterns were out, I whispered hints at their ears, lines of history, phrases of the classics. Some passed with flying colors. They burned incense for their ancestors, not knowing who had guided their hand.”

Liang Song’s broken mouth curled. “Still I could not leave. The ditch soaked me with meltwater each spring. Worms chewed my bones. My name faded from the registry.”

“Seventh leg: return. This year, they rebuilt the eastern wall. When the workers dug, they unearthed my coffin. I heard them shout. ‘A suicide from the exams, eh? Bad omen!’ They did not rebury me with care. They smashed the box, scattered what they did not want to touch. So my bones lie in the weeds, my spirit in the halls. The compound has become my tomb and my prison.

“Eighth leg: envy.” His eyes flared dull red. “I watch them come, year after year. Sons of merchants and magistrates, complaining that the cells are cramped, that the food is poor, that three days is long to write. They have warm cloaks and fat ink sticks, pockets full of coins for bribes. They pass, and their names are hung in gold characters. Who remembers Liang Song of Luo River?

“So I began to knock at the doors. To whisper at their windows: ‘Why study? Why try? The list is already written in silver.’ Some went mad, tearing up their essays. Others fled in the night. Their fear is a small repayment.”

Wen Shun listened, his own past failures weighing like lead. He thought of late nights under sputtering lamps, of his father’s quiet, the disappointed silence that filled each corner of their clay-walled home.

“Liang gongzi,” he said quietly, “if injustice chained you, then justice may yet unbind.”

The ghost gave a rasping laugh. “Justice? From men like Lord Zhao?”

“Lord Zhao is dead,” Wen Shun said. “Our current magistrate is Lord Wei. He is strict, but not known for greed. If he hears this, he may—”

“May what?” Liang Song snapped. “Give me a posthumous eighth place? Build a wooden tablet and bow to it twice a year? What use is that in the Yellow Springs?”

“For the living,” Wen Shun said, lifting his gaze to meet the ghost’s bulging eyes, “it may change the path. If the corruption is punished, future Liangs will not have to hang themselves in narrow cells. And for you… if your story is acknowledged by law, your resentment may lessen. You might find a boat across the dark river.”

The wind shifted. For a heartbeat, the ghost’s form wavered.

“You speak so confidently,” Liang murmured. “And what of you, Wen Shun? Failed three times, is it not so? If you expose this, you may bring the whole examination system here under scrutiny. They may cancel this year’s sitting. You may lose your last chance of youth.”

Wen Shun’s heart pounded. Images flashed: his father’s stooped back, his sisters’ calloused hands, the neighbors’ mutters. The hope that had kept him alive all these years was a small, tattered thing, but it burned stubbornly.

He inhaled the iron-cold air.

“If the ladder is rotten,” he said slowly, “what honor is there in climbing it? Better to mend it, even if I never reach the top. Our teacher in the village school once said: ‘To learn and not practice what is right is like not learning at all.’ Let me at least do this one sentence correctly.”

Liang Song stared at him for a long time. The ink in the stone had dried; cracks crazed its surface.

“Very well,” the ghost said at last, his voice thin as a breeze through reeds. “Go to your magistrate. Speak my name. Have them fetch what bones they can find, bury them with rites as for a wronged soul. Have them mark in the records that Liang Song of Luo River was unjustly treated by Examiners Zhao and his ilk. Invite my father’s shade to know.

“If all this is done, I will believe that the world of sun and dust can still hear the cries of the buried. Until then, I will walk here.”

He leaned forward, the cold of his presence stabbing through Wen Shun’s skull. “But heed this: if they mock you, if they turn this into another jest over wine, I will come to your bedside. Together we will wander these rows until the tiles crumble.”

Wen Shun’s mouth had gone dry. He bowed low enough that his forehead brushed the frozen brick.

“I will return by tomorrow night,” he said.

When he straightened, the corridor was empty. The inkstone was dry and cracked. Somewhere in the distance, a watchman beat the third night-watch drum.

***

Lord Wei listened, fingers steepled, as Wen Shun spoke in the cold morning light. The magistrate’s hall was warmer than the exam compound, but Wen Shun’s hands still shook; he clutched his sleeve to hide it.

“Liang Song,” Lord Wei repeated. “A suicide in the previous prefect’s term.”

He called for the old records. Clerks lugged out bamboo-bound volumes smelling of mold. After an hour, they found it: a brief note in a margin, written in a bored hand.

“‘One student, name Liang, hanged himself in cell 438 during last winter’s examination. Body interred near east wall. Omens consulted: no ill portents detected.’”

Lord Wei’s jaw tightened. He stood abruptly.

“Summon the gatekeeper. And the workmen who rebuilt the wall.”

By noon, several men knelt, trembling, in the courtyard. Under Lord Wei’s cold questions, the story of Liang Song’s shabby burial tumbled out. The lead worker admitted to breaking open the coffin and discarding scattered bones.

“That is enough,” Lord Wei said, disgust sharpening his voice. “We will search the grounds behind the east wall. Every fragment we find will be gathered. The rites must be performed.”

He turned to Wen Shun. “And the corruption. You implicate my predecessor, Lord Zhao, and his chief examiner. The ghost’s words cannot serve directly as evidence in a court of law. But missing silver leaves trails. Clerks remember. Servants talk. I will investigate this matter. If your account of Liang Song’s grievances proves true, we will memorialize it to the provincial office.”

Wen Shun bowed to the floor. “Even if Your Excellency only gives him proper burial, Liang Song’s soul will know.”

Lord Wei looked down at him. “You risked much, spending the night there. Why come back to tell me, when silence would have been safer?”

Wen Shun looked up, his eyes clear despite the exhaustion.

“My Lord, we are taught that officialdom is the road by which the worthy assist the people,” he said. “Yet the road is lined with bleached bones. If we avert our eyes from even one, what right have we to call ourselves scholars?”

Lord Wei’s gaze lingered. Then he nodded once.

“The rites will be performed tonight,” he said. “You will join them. A wronged scholar should be appeased by another scholar.”

***

As the sun slid toward the western hills, a procession wound out of Yanshui’s east gate: Lord Wei in court robes, clerks with scrolls and tall hats, Daoist acolytes with bells and wooden fish-drums, and Wen Shun carrying a brazier of incense.

Behind the examination compound, the ground was half-frozen and pitted with old construction. Laborers had marked a circle where they’d found shards of coffin-board and splinters of bone. Now, in the cold twilight, those fragments lay arranged on a blue cloth.

The Daoist priest chanted from the *Jade Register of the Dead*, calling on officials of the underworld to witness. Paper money fluttered up in gray flakes as assistants burned it, sending ghostly coin to the other side.

Lord Wei stepped forward and knelt, touching his forehead to the earth three times before the bones.

“Liang Song of Luo River,” he said, his voice carrying into the chill air, “hear this magistrate’s words. The world of yang acknowledges that you suffered grievance here. This district bears you apology. We now bury your remains within the protective wall, with incense and rites as for a wronged soul. May your spirit pass to where there is no cold nor hunger, and may you no longer wander among ink and dust.”

He rose. At his gesture, workers lowered a proper coffin into a freshly dug grave. Wen Shun stepped up, holding a tablet inscribed with four characters: “Tomb of the Wronged Scholar.”

He planted it in the earth as the soil thudded down.

When the last clod fell and the incense smoke twisted in the dimming air, a faint wind moved through the leafless willows. Wen Shun felt it brush his cheek: not the knife-like chill of the night before, but a cool, ordinary breeze.

In the slightest hush between the Daoist’s chants, he thought he heard a voice, very far away, reciting the opening line of the *Book of Songs*:

“Guan-guan cry the ospreys, on the islet in the river…”

Then it faded.

***

That night, Wen Shun went again to the examination compound, this time voluntarily. The two Zhang soldiers refused to leave the gate, muttering that one success should not tempt fate. Wen Shun walked alone through the rows of cells under a sky like hammered iron.

No ink stick scraped. No unseen fingers brushed his hair. The cells were only empty rooms, cold and dull, waiting to swallow the dreams of the living.

He stood before Liang Song’s old cubicle—cell 438—and bowed deeply.

“If you have truly gone on,” he said softly, “then listen to my foolish request from afar. Lend me a phrase or two, perhaps, when I sit here next month.”

Nothing answered. The silence felt, for the first time, like peace.

***

The investigation into Lord Zhao’s tenure uncovered a nest of bribery and favoritism. Ledgers showed inexplicable silver income; testimonies from embittered servants revealed years of purchased places on the lists. The provincial authorities, once alerted, made a show of righteousness: posthumous censures were issued, confiscated wealth used to repair schools and buy grain.

In the corner of one long memorial, however, a single line mentioned “Liang Song of Luo River, whose unjust death drew down misfortune and whose grievance has now been redressed
